n: The story opens in the unsettled era of the judges, when Israel often strayed and suffered. A famine pushes one Bethlehem family to move east across the Jordan to Moab, a neighboring nation often hostile to Israel.

f.g: Bethlehem (“house of bread”) in Judah, distinguishing it from a Bethlehem in Zebulun. Later the birthplace of David and of Jesus.

n: The family members are named. Their names carry meaning: Elimelech means “my God is king” and Naomi means “pleasant,” which becomes important when Naomi later asks to be renamed.

f.g: Ephrath or Ephratah was an older name for the Bethlehem area.

n: Tragedy strikes: Naomi's husband dies in a foreign land, leaving her a widow far from home with only her two sons to support her.
Naomi's sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. The family stays in Moab about ten years, putting down roots outside the covenant land.
Both sons die as well, so Naomi is left with no husband and no sons. In that world, this meant no income, no protection, and no one to carry on the family name.

f.g: Widows without sons were among the most vulnerable people in ancient society; the law repeatedly commands care for them.

n: Naomi hears that the famine back home has ended. The text credits the Lord with sending food again, a quiet reminder that God is at work behind the scenes of this whole story.

f.g: To “visit” here means to come to someone's aid with care and blessing.

n: Naomi sets out for Judah, and both daughters-in-law begin the journey with her, showing their affection for her.
On the road Naomi urges the young women to go back to their own mothers' homes. She blesses them, praying the Lord will show them the same kindness they have shown her family.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — loyal, covenant love; faithful kindness that goes beyond duty. It is the key word of the book of Ruth.

n: Naomi hopes they will each find “rest” — the security of a new home and husband. The farewell is tearful because they truly love one another.

f.g: Here, settled security and safety in a household.

n: At first both women insist on staying with Naomi and going to her people.
Naomi reasons with them: she has no more sons to give them as husbands. She is thinking of the custom where a brother would marry his dead brother's widow to keep the family line alive.

f.w: that they may be your husbands
f.g: A reference to levirate marriage, where a brother-in-law married a childless widow.

n: Naomi presses her point: she is too old to remarry, and even if she married that very night and had sons, the timing would be impossible.
Would they wait decades for babies to grow up? Naomi feels her losses as the Lord's hand against her, and she does not want the young women to share her hardship.
After more tears, Orpah kisses Naomi goodbye and turns back, a sensible choice. But Ruth holds tight to Naomi and will not let go.

f.g: clung, held fast. The same word describes a husband cleaving to his wife.

n: Naomi points out that Orpah has returned to her people and her gods, and urges Ruth to do the same. Choosing Naomi would mean leaving Moab's religion behind.
Ruth answers with one of scripture's most beautiful vows of loyalty. She binds herself not just to Naomi but to Israel and to Israel's God — a true conversion.
Ruth's commitment is for life and beyond: she will even be buried in Naomi's land. She seals it with a solemn oath in the name of the LORD, Israel's God.

f.w: the LORD do so to me, and more also
f.g: A standard oath formula: may God punish me severely if I break this promise.

n: Seeing that Ruth's mind is firmly made up, Naomi stops arguing.
The two women reach Bethlehem, and the whole town buzzes. The women of the town can hardly recognize Naomi after ten hard years.
Naomi asks to be called Mara (“bitter”) instead of Naomi (“pleasant”). Her grief is honest; scripture allows her to voice her pain to and about God.

f.g: Hebrew Shaddai, an ancient title for God.

n: She left with a husband and sons and returns with nothing — or so she thinks. Readers notice the irony: she has come home with Ruth, who will become her greatest blessing.

f.g: Naomi feels as if God has brought a case against her.

n: The chapter closes with hope: they arrive just as barley harvest begins in spring, setting the stage for Ruth's gleaning and for the Lord's provision.

f.g: Barley ripened first, around April, followed by wheat a few weeks later.
